simple answer - you can’t. Our system is so broken and so entrenched that it is NOT possible to fix it.
To make education work again in the US the system has to be completely discarded and replaced with a working system. The following minimum things must happen:
The stranglehold on education by the teachers unions must be broken - I am NOT advocating the ‘breaking’ of the unions - they serve a legitimate purpose and are a legal right of the teachers. I am advocating the curtailment of their power in regards to the “how” of the way education is administered in the US.
The spurious and frivolous use of the courts by parents to shape schools to their individual liking and often in opposition to the community standards needs to be curtailed by law or by punishing countersuits. Just because your Johnny can’t wear his hair in blue or wear a shirt that says “f*** you* doesn’t mean his creativity is stifled or that his 1st amendment rights are restricted - in fact his 1st amendment rights are naturally restricted in a school - that’s the point.
The ridiculous adherence to an agricultural schedule for our education system is a dinosaur that simply has to go. No business model or efficiency adviser would advocate building multi-million dollar facilities and then let them sit idle for a fourth of the year.

# How can K-12 education systems better engage students who process information much faster than their peers?
Textbooks need to go. There is simply no reason in the current world to publish unbelievably expensive textbooks that hold essentially the same information as the previous edition. So some new history has been added - what changed in the previous 2000 years of history? Besides in a world of inexpensive Nooks and devices, schools only need license access to textbook information (and only then because it is cheaper and easier than having the teachers assemble their own from the internet). What schools do need is workbooks, but in many cases families can either buy their own or the school can provide a sliding scale purchase rate based on family income. Workbooks are still important because students need to learn to write - not every assignment can be typed on a tablet.
Sports need to go private. Expenditures of time and money on primary school athletics are a distraction from mission (education) and a diversion of funding. Traveling teams and private or booster support will sustain sports programs and organizations like state athletic associations can ensure that participants continue to maintain grades, etc. and for those that believe that this will eliminate opportunity for disadvantaged children really do not understand sports. Talent will always be recruited - and sponsors will always pay to support those talents. Besides the only sports that need to go are the inter-school ones. Intramural sports in the schools serve a purpose of exercise and the same ‘team’ oriented and recognition goals, with minimal costs associated.
Curriculum needs to be examined carefully. Elementary students need to acquire a minimum amount of knowledge to be effective in later years. Creativity and critical thinking are NOT elementary school student goals. Rote collection of base knowledge is critical so that critical thinking skills can be exercised later.
Knowledge base needs to build year to year not repeat over and over. Adult students would literally revolt if they had to study the civil war or any other historical event every year or every other year in college without any change in the focus. yet we teach history and social studies that are essentially the same all through the primary grades. Math is a disaster - abstract math is taught too early and then in an overly complicated system. We DO NOT have to reinvent the wheel here just so someone can have recognition. The world is using methods that the US used to use and out performing us on standardized tests.

# How can K-12 education systems better engage students who process information much faster than their peers?
Lastly we need to bring costs into line - which may mean salary adjustments for teachers and especially administrators. The system has to be able to expand to include community college level for all students and it needs to do so with about the same amount of money. Every student needs to go on to community college in or near their home town as part of primary education. this serves two main goals - first every student has a marketable skill or job potential upon graduation and every student that goes on to college has shaved a significant portion of their future debt off of the bill.
There are a lot more details and this is something I am passionate about. I will not go on here though, because - agree or disagree with me, I am grateful that you have read this far.

# How can K-12 education systems better engage students who process information much faster than their peers?
Schools do take large numbers of students and group them together by age under the theory that they will develop roughly the same. While this holds true for a fair number of students, there are those who require additional time and those who develop faster or whose talents allow them to learn at a faster rate. These students are not as well served by the traditional system, although flexible class assignment, testing opt outs, gifted and tented programs, AP classes and differentiated instruction within a classroom can reduce or eliminate much of the issue if the school embraces, financially supports and makes use of alternatives such as these. Some programs allow students to graduate from high school at age 15 if they have completed all requirements including testing out of some of them.

Once I am sure that the work was completed appropriately and not just rushed to get it done, then students who finish before others may choose a book from my “Reading Resources”. The resources I have collected are related to the subject that I teach (science) but are at a very wide range of reading levels, including some that are mostly pictures (coffee table type books).
The reason for the range in levels is two-fold. First, I have many students in my 7th grade classes who functionally read at the primary level. They struggle to read our grade level textbook, so these books are engaging for them. Second, I do not believe in punishing early finishers with more work. Choosing something easier to read or more challenging is their choice. Many of them enjoy the simple books because they cover topics not directly related to the curriculum, but are great fun to read about anyway.

I taught ideas found in the literature of the critical thinking movement started by Richard Paul and Linda Elder (husband and wife) from Sonama California. Also, I found my old college text “Creative and Critical Thinking” by Edgar V. Moore a good guide as well. Both were very well organized and fit well in the course I taught in high school. Both were based on real life decision making and were very useful.
The heart of Paul and Elder’s work was the deceptively simple statement: “All thinking has a PURPOSE, with a POINT OF VIEW, is based on ASSUMPTIONS which have IMPLICATIONS and CONSEQUENCES. With FACTS, DATA, and our EXPERIENCES, we use INFERENCES and JUDGEMENTS based on CONCEPTS to SOLVE PROBLEMS and MAKE DECISIONS.” The power of this cannot be overstated. It provides students the ability to break apart and analyze any thinking system by using key concepts.
Edgar V. Moore modeled his entire book around a five step decision making process: IDENTIFY AND DEFINE THE PROBLEM, GATHER INFORMATION, FORM TENTATIVE HYPOTHESES, TEST TENTATIVE HYPOTHESES, EVALUATE AND DECIDE. Each phase was filled with relevant and practical information and examples. He defined the differences between facts and beliefs. He used Aristotle’s syllogisms to analyze hypotheses’ reliability (valid plus true equals reliable) and taught how to use three points of view to sell a product which he called “influencing decision making”: self image, frame of reference, and value system. It worked very well in application.

I taught ideas found in the literature of the critical thinking movement started by Richard Paul and Linda Elder (husband and wife) from Sonama California. Also, I found my old college text “Creative and Critical Thinking” by Edgar V. Moore a good guide as well. Both were very well organized and fit well in the course I taught in high school. Both were based on real life decision making and were very useful.
The heart of Paul and Elder’s work was the deceptively simple statement: “All thinking has a PURPOSE, with a POINT OF VIEW, is based on ASSUMPTIONS which have IMPLICATIONS and CONSEQUENCES. With FACTS, DATA, and our EXPERIENCES, we use INFERENCES and JUDGEMENTS based on CONCEPTS to SOLVE PROBLEMS and MAKE DECISIONS.” The power of this cannot be overstated. It provides students the ability to break apart and analyze any thinking system by using key concepts.
Edgar V. Moore modeled his entire book around a five step decision making process: IDENTIFY AND DEFINE THE PROBLEM, GATHER INFORMATION, FORM TENTATIVE HYPOTHESES, TEST TENTATIVE HYPOTHESES, EVALUATE AND DECIDE. Each phase was filled with relevant and practical information and examples. He defined the differences between facts and beliefs. He used Aristotle’s syllogisms to analyze hypotheses’ reliability (valid plus true equals reliable) and taught how to use three points of view to sell a product which he called “influencing decision making”: self image, frame of reference, and value system. It worked very well in application.

When you grow up broke you take the money. Phil Knight said I can’t offer you the same money but I can give you stock. I didn’t even know what stocks was at that time. So I passed.” Those Nike shares today would be worth an estimated $5 billion. But here is the thing about Magic Johnson. Even that decision couldn’t stop him. In 1995 he partnered with Starbucks to open 125 stores in underserved urban communities that corporate America had completely ignored. When he sold his stake in 2010 he walked away with $75 million. [[](https://www.instagram.com/broke.or.billionaire) broke.or.bill... 16.3K In 1979 Nike co-founder Phil Knight approached 19 year old Magic Johnson with a shoe deal. Nike was just getting started. They couldn’t match what Converse was offering in cash. So Knight offered him something different. Stock. Magic said no. His own words — “Converse offered me the most money. When you grow up broke you take the money. Phil Knight said I can’t offer you the same money but I can give you stock. I didn’t even know what stocks was at that time. So I passed.” Those Nike shares today would be worth an estimated $5 billion. But here is the thing about Magic Johnson. Even that decision couldn’t stop him. In 1995 he partnered with Starbucks to open 125 stores in underserved urban communities that corporate America had completely ignored. When he sold his stake in 2010 he walked away with $75 million. He invested $50 million into the Los Angeles Dodgers as part of a $2.15 billion purchase — the largest sports franchise sale in history at the time. He owns stakes in the Washington Commanders. The LA Sparks. LA Football Club. He acquired a 60% controlling stake in EquiTrust Life Insurance — a company now managing over $26 billion in assets. But the detail nobody talks about? He started his career as a teenager cleaning office floors in Lansing Michigan. He would sneak into the top floor executive suite and sit in the CEO’s chair — just to feel what it was like to be in charge. Net worth today — $1.6 billion. He passed on $5 billion in Nike stock at 19 years old. And still became a billionaire. Is Magic Johnson the greatest businessman in sports history? Why are student numbers falling at secondary level and what can we do to bring children back to school? I briefly commented ... in this [Channel 24](https://www.facebook.com/channel24bd.tv?__cft__[0]=AZjvA2Q1sSS7nPFGW5gmRJq10c9PX4XdR28XG_80zeW5Y4KrpwlJQbfmAZZjOSf8tFrtwc_JOYLfiYeOZEJcLA6S3SKfmf8aE_V6MB1PhAYgnBuDXaX0Xjnqn_BF0l1oEF_C5ORIcHtGt02Afwsbkaf-EA&__tn__=-]K-R) report on the worrying decline of more than 1.6 million students in post-primary education over the past two years.
The long COVID school closure was followed by further disruptions. Weak foundational learning in pre-secondary grades, financial pressure on families and concerns about education quality can all place children’s education at risk.
But a fall in enrolment does not mean that every missing student has dropped out. We need to understand how many have left education altogether, how many have moved to another stream, and why. We also need targeted support for children who have fallen behind and families struggling to keep them in school.

Why are student numbers falling at secondary level and what can we do to bring children back to school? I briefly commented ... in this [Channel 24](https://www.facebook.com/channel24bd.tv?__cft__[0]=AZjvA2Q1sSS7nPFGW5gmRJq10c9PX4XdR28XG_80zeW5Y4KrpwlJQbfmAZZjOSf8tFrtwc_JOYLfiYeOZEJcLA6S3SKfmf8aE_V6MB1PhAYgnBuDXaX0Xjnqn_BF0l1oEF_C5ORIcHtGt02Afwsbkaf-EA&__tn__=-]K-R) report on the worrying decline of more than 1.6 million students in post-primary education over the past two years.
The long COVID school closure was followed by further disruptions. Weak foundational learning in pre-secondary grades, financial pressure on families and concerns about education quality can all place children’s education at risk.
But a fall in enrolment does not mean that every missing student has dropped out. We need to understand how many have left education altogether, how many have moved to another stream, and why. We also need targeted support for children who have fallen behind and families struggling to keep them in school.

[[](https://www.instagram.com/richmondforum) richmondforum 1,380 Today is National Speech & Debate Education Day, a celebration of one of the most powerful classrooms there is: the exchange of ideas. Speech and debate teaches students how to think critically, argue thoughtfully, and listen to perspectives different from their own. The results speak for themselves: higher GPAs, stronger analytical skills, increased attendance, and a remarkable 98% high school graduation rate among participants. Here in Richmond, the Richmond Forum Speech & Debate Initiative has been working since 2018 to bring those opportunities to more students across our region. Today, speech and debate programs are active in 91% of public high schools and nearly a quarter of middle schools in Richmond, Chesterfield, Henrico, Hanover, and Petersburg. And this summer, Richmond will become the national stage for these extraordinary young people. From June 14–19, 2026, our city will host the National Speech & Debate Tournament, welcoming 7,000 students and thousands more coaches, judges, and families from across the country. For one week, our schools, theaters, and convention center will be filled with ideas, arguments, stories, and the unmistakable energy of the next generation learning how to use their voices. Learn more and support Richmond’s effort to host the tournament: www.richmondforum.org/2026](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DVjCH2sFV3V/?utm_source=popular_topic_grid)

Title: 16K views · 327 reactions | “LET’S PAY OUR TEACHERS DECENT SALARIES”: A stark call for African governments to invest in teachers has taken centre stage at the Pan-African Conference on Teacher Education and Development (PACTED) in Ezulwini.

Dr Dennis Sinyolo, Director of Education International Africa, says he has visited countries across the continent where teachers are not paid regularly, including one situation where, he says, teachers have gone two years without receiving their salaries while still being expected to report to class and teach.

“Let’s pay our teachers decent salaries so that they can focus on what they know how to do best, to teach,” Sinyolo said, stressing that educators should not have to worry about where their next meal will come from.

He also took aim at the gap between policy and implementation, saying Africa has “great policies on paper but very little action on the ground.”

The remarks come on World Teachers’ Day, as delegates gather in Eswatini to deliberate on transforming the teaching profession, including teacher professionalism, qualifications, mobility and the role of artificial intelligence in education.

Sinyolo’s message is clear: Celebrating teachers must go hand in hand with valuing, supporting and paying them. | Times of Eswatini

# Union Budget 2019-20: First Take | ‘FM Nirmala Sitharaman is no less a magician!’
## Predictably, infrastructure retains its pride of place amongst the government’s priorities, while disinvestment finds its customary mention, as it has for several years.
Updated  - July 05, 2019 09:43 pm IST
T.T. Srinivasaraghavan
READ LATER
SEE ALL Remove
T.T. Srinivasaraghavan, Managing Director, Sundaram Finance.
I have long held that the most difficult and thankless job of all, in our country, is that of the Union Finance Minister! Meeting the endless expectations of business, farmers, industry lobbies, foreign portfolio investors, stock market players and the common man, requires the FM to be a magician, no less. How does one reconcile the conflicting demands of those seeking tax cuts and increased subsidies on the one hand with those who seek increased government investment in infrastructure, bank recapitalisation and alleviation of rural distress, on the other? But it is this brave task that India’s first lady Finance Minister has undertaken.
At a broad level, FDI seems to have taken centre stage, seeking perhaps to offer an alternative to China, as uncertainty continues over the Sino-U.S. trade war. Predictably, infrastructure retains its pride of place amongst the government’s priorities, while disinvestment finds its customary mention, as it has for several years. Also unsurprisingly, gas, electricity, toilets (GET) remains high on the agenda, given how much of a factor it was in the recently-concluded elections. But over the next few days and weeks, commentators and experts will have a field day dissecting the budget, while the stock market will likely go through its own gyrations!
Turning specifically to the financial sector, there are several noteworthy proposals, both on the capital markets front and the regulatory/taxation front. The proposal to permit investments made by FIIs/FPIs in debt securities issued by Infrastructure Debt Fund – Non-Bank Finance Companies (IDF-NBFCs) to be transferred/sold to any domestic investor within the specified lock-in period and allow AA rated bonds as collateral, should hopefully kick off the long talked about deepening of bond markets. The move to bring HFCs under RBI supervision is also very logical.

# Union Budget 2019-20: First Take | ‘FM Nirmala Sitharaman is no less a magician!’
## Predictably, infrastructure retains its pride of place amongst the government’s priorities, while disinvestment finds its customary mention, as it has for several years.
After months of uninformed discourse on the ‘NBFC crisis’, it was both refreshing and reassuring to hear the FM acknowledge in unequivocal terms that NBFCs play a key role in the country’s economic growth and the fundamentally sound ones should continue to get funding from banks and mutual funds. The one-time partial credit guarantee offered to public sector banks for purchase of ‘high-rated pooled assets’ of financially sound NBFCs amounting to ₹1 lakh crore in FY20 is a good confidence restoring move, while the removal of the Debenture Redemption Reserve for NBFCs opens up a viable avenue of resource raising for well-run NBFCs. For 20 years and more, NBFCs have sought parity with banks in respect of taxability of income on non-performing assets, under Section 43 D of the Income Tax Act. For those of us who fought this long battle, this comes as a really sweet reward!
Perhaps one of the least noticed announcements is the one regarding “an expert committee to study the current situation relating to long-term finance and our past experience with development finance institutions, and recommend the structure and required flow of funds through development finance institutions.” One can’t help but feel that the IL&FS fiasco might have never happened had the DFIs such as IDBI and ICICI not been swept away by the fashionable clamour for Universal Banking!
Above all, the honourable Finance Minister did not once refer to the non-banking finance companies as ‘shadow banks’. If only for this, we owe her a debt of gratitude.
_(TT Srinivasaraghavan, Sundaram Finance MD)_

# Union Budget 2019-20: First Take | ‘FM Nirmala Sitharaman is no less a magician!’
## Predictably, infrastructure retains its pride of place amongst the government’s priorities, while disinvestment finds its customary mention, as it has for several years.
Updated  - July 05, 2019 09:43 pm IST
T.T. Srinivasaraghavan
READ LATER
SEE ALL Remove
T.T. Srinivasaraghavan, Managing Director, Sundaram Finance.
I have long held that the most difficult and thankless job of all, in our country, is that of the Union Finance Minister! Meeting the endless expectations of business, farmers, industry lobbies, foreign portfolio investors, stock market players and the common man, requires the FM to be a magician, no less. How does one reconcile the conflicting demands of those seeking tax cuts and increased subsidies on the one hand with those who seek increased government investment in infrastructure, bank recapitalisation and alleviation of rural distress, on the other? But it is this brave task that India’s first lady Finance Minister has undertaken.
At a broad level, FDI seems to have taken centre stage, seeking perhaps to offer an alternative to China, as uncertainty continues over the Sino-U.S. trade war. Predictably, infrastructure retains its pride of place amongst the government’s priorities, while disinvestment finds its customary mention, as it has for several years. Also unsurprisingly, gas, electricity, toilets (GET) remains high on the agenda, given how much of a factor it was in the recently-concluded elections. But over the next few days and weeks, commentators and experts will have a field day dissecting the budget, while the stock market will likely go through its own gyrations!
Turning specifically to the financial sector, there are several noteworthy proposals, both on the capital markets front and the regulatory/taxation front. The proposal to permit investments made by FIIs/FPIs in debt securities issued by Infrastructure Debt Fund – Non-Bank Finance Companies (IDF-NBFCs) to be transferred/sold to any domestic investor within the specified lock-in period and allow AA rated bonds as collateral, should hopefully kick off the long talked about deepening of bond markets. The move to bring HFCs under RBI supervision is also very logical.

# Union Budget 2019-20: First Take | ‘FM Nirmala Sitharaman is no less a magician!’
## Predictably, infrastructure retains its pride of place amongst the government’s priorities, while disinvestment finds its customary mention, as it has for several years.
After months of uninformed discourse on the ‘NBFC crisis’, it was both refreshing and reassuring to hear the FM acknowledge in unequivocal terms that NBFCs play a key role in the country’s economic growth and the fundamentally sound ones should continue to get funding from banks and mutual funds. The one-time partial credit guarantee offered to public sector banks for purchase of ‘high-rated pooled assets’ of financially sound NBFCs amounting to ₹1 lakh crore in FY20 is a good confidence restoring move, while the removal of the Debenture Redemption Reserve for NBFCs opens up a viable avenue of resource raising for well-run NBFCs. For 20 years and more, NBFCs have sought parity with banks in respect of taxability of income on non-performing assets, under Section 43 D of the Income Tax Act. For those of us who fought this long battle, this comes as a really sweet reward!
Perhaps one of the least noticed announcements is the one regarding “an expert committee to study the current situation relating to long-term finance and our past experience with development finance institutions, and recommend the structure and required flow of funds through development finance institutions.” One can’t help but feel that the IL&FS fiasco might have never happened had the DFIs such as IDBI and ICICI not been swept away by the fashionable clamour for Universal Banking!
Above all, the honourable Finance Minister did not once refer to the non-banking finance companies as ‘shadow banks’. If only for this, we owe her a debt of gratitude.
_(TT Srinivasaraghavan, Sundaram Finance MD)_

Nirmala Sitharaman a native of Trichy, was born to Shri N. Sitaraman (a railway employee) and Savitri.She did schooling in Savithri Vidyasala, and obtained a B.A. degree from same institution, Seethalakshmi Ramaswamy College, Trichy, and an MA degree in economics from JNU Delhi in 1980[ followed by a Ph.D in the Indo-European textile trade within the GATT framework and MPhil. Nirmala then served at Price Waterhouse Coopers as a Senior Manager and later for the BBC world service. She is one of the founding directors of Pranava school in Hyderabad, before joining BJP in 2004.

Title: ET NOW on Instagram: "Vangmayi Parakala, the daughter of India’s Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman, is a person who has chosen to lead a life away from the public eye, despite her prominent family background. Though she is connected to some of India’s most influential political figures, Vangmayi has managed to carve out her own path, both in her career and personal life.

Born in Chennai, Vangmayi comes from a family deeply entrenched in politics and academia. Her mother, Nirmala Sitharaman, is one of India’s most prominent political leaders, currently serving as the country's Finance Minister. Her father, Parakala Prabhakar, is a well-known political economist and social commentator who has held important roles, including serving as the Communications Advisor to the Andhra Pradesh Government, where he held a cabinet rank.

Vangmayi Parakala has a strong academic background. She completed her Bachelor’s and Master’s degrees in English Literature from the University of Delhi, further honing her intellectual capabilities. Her passion for storytelling and communication led her to pursue a Master of Science in Journalism from the prestigious Medill School of Journalism at Northwestern University in the United States. This education set the stage for her career in writing and journalism.

In June 2023, Vangmayi Parakala married Pratik Doshi in a private ceremony held in Bengaluru. Pratik Doshi is a key aide to Prime Minister Narendra Modi and has been with him since 2014.

Nirmala Sitharaman a native of Trichy, was born to Shri N. Sitaraman (a railway employee) and Savitri.She did schooling in Savithri Vidyasala, and obtained a B.A. degree from same institution, Seethalakshmi Ramaswamy College, Trichy, and an MA degree in economics from JNU Delhi in 1980[ followed by a Ph.D in the Indo-European textile trade within the GATT framework and MPhil. Nirmala then served at Price Waterhouse Coopers as a Senior Manager and later for the BBC world service. She is one of the founding directors of Pranava school in Hyderabad, before joining BJP in 2004.
